line 24: With the musical filled with humor, romance, great characters, heart and lots and lots of music, it is vital that the audience can hear every note, every lyric and every perfectly timed joke if it is going to connect with them. That is where Tony-nominated sound designer Walter Trarbach comes in. His work on Schmigadoon! earned him his second Tony nomination for Sound Design of a Musical.
line 25: It is not simply about recreating the look of an old-fashioned musical. It is about making the audience feel what it was like to experience one, while using every tool available to a modern Broadway production.
line 26: “Well, in terms of big musicals, we did this one on a very short timeline, which I think is kind of a testament to the confidence that the director and the producer had in the project and how well developed it was. Normally, there’s a longer load-in period where we put the equipment in the theater. There’s a longer tech period. There’s a longer preview period. And this we did the whole thing pretty fast, I’ll say. So
line 33: That philosophy was followed throughout the show’s sound design. “We don’t really use any of the tricks that you would use in a more produced rock album or show. We kind of just try and rely on the orchestra to blend internally and we try to present that to the audience,” he continued. “So we don’t use compression. We don’t use a lot of reverb. There are no vocal tracks. There’s no metronome. The musical director Ste
line 34: Trarbach is at times the air traffic controller of sound, taking the sound created by the performers and musicians and carefully deciding how those sounds reach every person in the theater.
line 36: “It’s almost like curating exactly what the audience should be hearing out of everything that’s done on stage,” explained Trarbach. “We put microphones on every actor, every musician. I think there may be like 18 or 20 microphones in the percussion area alone because they’ve got all these little things. Then we just kind of take it moment by moment and we try to mix the songs, try and make them sound a little better 
line 37: For such a sound-focused job, a surprising amount of physicality was required of Trarbach, as he had to move around the theater from seat to seat to experience that difference for himself because there is no single place in a Broadway theater from which the audience experiences the show in the same way audibly. A sound that works perfectly in one seat can feel completely different several rows away.
line 38: “[The sound] definitely changes in every part of the theater. So in every performance basically, I’d get a different seat from management. I’d sit in this place, then I’d sit in the next place. And sometimes if it’s good, like after an act I’ll leave and go to a different part of the theater and kind of see what it’s like there.”
line 41: The problem was not simply making sure the jokes could be heard. The audience’s reaction could actually change the rhythm of the show.
line 42: “And everything changed when there was laughter, and that changed the entire rhythm of the show, obviously for the better, but it also… if there’s kind of a rolling laugh it would step on jokes. line 43: Sometimes, the solution was not something Trarbach could fix from behind the sound console and the show needed to be slightly reworked to ensure that the audience reactions did not step on the joke or the emotion of the show.

line 46: It is another part of what makes live theater so different from film. There is no opportunity to simply move the camera closer or cut around a problem. Everything has to happen in the room, in real time, and it goes both ways, with the audience participating in the experience. If you lose the audience’s energy, that reverberates back onto the stage.
line 47: “If you were doing a movie, you can do close shots and frame the audience’s attention that way. But in theater we have to do a lot of it with lighting and sound. So we rely a lot on the lighting designer to train the eye of the audience. But we also, in terms of sound, want to keep everything moving along and keep it cohesive.”
line 48: Keeping the cohesion and retaining the natural feel of the story becomes quite technical. While it feels effortless, there is a precision to the sound design that extends throughout.
